section.title: The Transfiguration and True Greatness
section.sectionRationale: On the way to the cross Jesus is unveiled in glory on the mountain, and the Father's voice commands, Listen to Him. Coming down, He casts out a spirit His disciples could not, drawing out a father's honest cry of faith. He predicts His death a second time, and then repeatedly overturns the disciples' hunger for greatness: true greatness is servanthood, the kingdom belongs to those who welcome children, and sin must be dealt with ruthlessly.
section.thesis: The suffering Son of Man is the beloved Son in glory whom the Father commands us to heed, and those who follow Him must trade rivalry for servanthood, receive the lowly, guard the little ones, and cut off whatever leads to sin, living at peace as salt in the world.
section.frameNote: Six beats: the transfiguration and the Father's voice; the question about Elijah; the boy with an unclean spirit; the second Passion prediction; true greatness and welcoming children; and warnings about causing stumbling, radical dealing with sin, and being salt.

units.label: The transfiguration
units.note: This is My beloved Son, listen to Him

verses.text: After six days Jesus took with Him Peter, James, and John, and led them up a high mountain by themselves. There He was {{metamorphoo|transfigured}} before them.
His clothes became radiantly white, brighter than any launderer on earth could bleach them.
And Elijah and Moses appeared before them, talking with Jesus.
Peter said to Jesus, “Rabbi, it is good for us to be here. Let us put up three shelters, one for You, one for Moses, and one for Elijah.”
For they were all so terrified that Peter did not know what else to say.
Then a cloud appeared and enveloped them, and a voice came from the cloud: “This is My beloved Son. Listen to Him!”
Suddenly, when they looked around, they saw no one with them except Jesus.
As they were coming down the mountain, Jesus admonished them not to tell anyone what they had seen until the Son of Man had risen from the dead.
So they kept this matter to themselves, discussing what it meant to rise from the dead.
And they asked Jesus, “Why do the scribes say that Elijah must come first?”
He replied, “Elijah does indeed come first, and he restores all things. Why then is it written that the Son of Man must suffer many things and be rejected?
But I tell you that Elijah has indeed come, and they have done to him whatever they wished, just as it is written about him.”

units.label: The boy with an unclean spirit
units.note: I do believe; help my unbelief

verses.text: When they returned to the other disciples, they saw a large crowd around them, and scribes arguing with them.
As soon as all the people saw Jesus, they were filled with awe and ran to greet Him.
“What are you disputing with them?” He asked.
Someone in the crowd replied, “Teacher, I brought You my son, who has a spirit that makes him mute.
Whenever it seizes him, it throws him to the ground. He foams at the mouth, gnashes his teeth, and becomes rigid. I asked Your disciples to drive it out, but they were unable.”
“O unbelieving generation!” Jesus replied. “How long must I remain with you? How long must I put up with you? Bring the boy to Me.”
So they brought him, and seeing Jesus, the spirit immediately threw the boy into a convulsion. He fell to the ground and rolled around, foaming at the mouth.
Jesus asked the boy’s father, “How long has this been with him?” “From childhood,” he said.
“It often throws him into the fire or into the water, trying to kill him. But if You can do anything, have compassion on us and help us.”
“If You can?” echoed Jesus. “All things are possible to him who believes!”
Immediately the boy’s father cried out, “I do believe; help my unbelief!”
When Jesus saw that a crowd had come running, He rebuked the unclean spirit. “You deaf and mute spirit,” He said, “I command you to come out and never enter him again.”
After shrieking and convulsing him violently, the spirit came out. The boy became like a corpse, so that many said, “He is dead.”
But Jesus took him by the hand and helped him to his feet, and he stood up.
After Jesus had gone into the house, His disciples asked Him privately, “Why couldn’t we drive it out?”
Jesus answered, “This kind cannot come out, except by prayer.”

units.label: The second Passion prediction
units.note: delivered into the hands of men

verses.text: Going on from there, they passed through Galilee. But Jesus did not want anyone to know,
because He was teaching His disciples. He told them, “The Son of Man will be delivered into the hands of men. They will kill Him, and after three days He will rise.”
But they did not understand this statement, and they were afraid to ask Him about it.

units.label: True greatness and welcoming children
units.note: the last of all and the servant of all

verses.text: Then they came to Capernaum. While Jesus was in the house, He asked them, “What were you discussing on the way?”
But they were silent, for on the way they had been arguing about which of them was the greatest.
Sitting down, Jesus called the Twelve and said, “If anyone wants to be first, he must be the last of all and the {{diakonos|servant}} of all.”
Then He had a little child stand among them. Taking the child in His arms, He said to them,
“Whoever welcomes one of these little children in My name welcomes Me, and whoever welcomes Me welcomes not only Me, but the One who sent Me.”
John said to Him, “Teacher, we saw someone else driving out demons in Your name, and we tried to stop him, because he does not accompany us.”
“Do not stop him,” Jesus replied. “For no one who performs a miracle in My name can turn around and speak evil of Me.
For whoever is not against us is for us.
Indeed, if anyone gives you even a cup of water because you bear the name of Christ, truly I tell you, he will never lose his reward.
But if anyone causes one of these little ones who believe in Me to {{skandalizo|stumble}}, it would be better for him to have a large millstone hung around his neck and to be thrown into the sea.
If your hand causes you to sin, cut it off. It is better for you to enter life crippled than to have two hands and go into {{gehenna|hell}}, into the unquenchable fire.
If your foot causes you to sin, cut it off. It is better for you to enter life lame than to have two feet and be thrown into hell.
And if your eye causes you to sin, pluck it out. It is better for you to enter the kingdom of God with one eye than to have two eyes and be thrown into hell,
where ‘their worm never dies, and the fire is never quenched.’
For everyone will be salted with fire.
{{halas|Salt}} is good, but if the salt loses its saltiness, with what will you season it? Have salt among yourselves, and be at peace with one another.”

metamorphoo.gloss: To transform, to change form. On the mountain Jesus is transfigured, His inner glory shining through His body and clothes. It is a glimpse of who He truly is and of the glory that lies beyond the cross, confirming that the suffering Son is the glorious Son of God.

diakonos.gloss: A servant, one who waits on others. Jesus overturns the world's ladder of greatness: to be first in the kingdom is to be last and the servant of all. Greatness is measured by lowly service, modelled by the Son of Man who came to serve and give His life.

skandalizo.gloss: To cause to stumble, to trip into sin. Jesus warns with terrible seriousness against causing one of His little ones to stumble, and against whatever in ourselves leads us into sin; the danger of sin is grave enough to warrant the most drastic response.

gehenna.gloss: Hell, from the Valley of Hinnom outside Jerusalem, a place of burning and refuse associated with judgment. Jesus uses it for the final judgment of the unrepentant, the unquenchable fire, underscoring how seriously sin must be taken and how real the stakes are.

halas.gloss: Salt, used to preserve, purify, and flavour, and a token of covenant. Disciples are to have salt in themselves, a purifying, preserving character tested by fire, and to keep peace with one another rather than the rivalry that had just consumed them.

basic.context: Six days after foretelling His death, Jesus takes Peter, James, and John up a mountain and is transfigured before them, blazing with glory, with Moses and Elijah beside Him, until the Father's voice says, This is My beloved Son, listen to Him. Coming down, Jesus casts out a spirit the disciples could not, and the boy's father cries, I believe, help my unbelief. Jesus predicts His death again, but the disciples, instead of grasping it, argue about who is the greatest. Jesus answers with a series of reversals: to be first is to be servant of all, to welcome a child is to welcome Him, no one who works in His name is against Him, causing a little one to stumble is dreadful, and sin must be cut out ruthlessly. He ends by calling them to be salt and to be at peace with one another.
basic.hermeneutics: The glory of the transfiguration confirms the message of the cross; the Father's command, listen to Him, endorses the suffering path Jesus just announced. The rest of the chapter shows how badly the disciples misunderstand: while Jesus speaks of dying, they compete for status. Jesus repeatedly inverts human values, defining greatness as service and warning that the stakes of sin are eternal.
basic.originalLanguages: Jesus is metamorphoo, transfigured, in glory. He teaches that the great must be diakonos, servant, of all. He warns against causing little ones to skandalizo, stumble, and against sin that leads to gehenna, hell. And He calls disciples to be halas, salt, at peace with one another.
basic.typology: Moses and Elijah, the law and the prophets, appear with Jesus and then fade, leaving Him alone: He is the one they pointed to. The transfiguration on the mountain echoes God's glory on Sinai. John the Baptist is the promised Elijah who suffers before the Son of Man suffers.
basic.christ: Jesus is the beloved Son, radiant in divine glory, to whom the Father says listen. He is the servant-King who defines greatness by lowliness, and the Son of Man who will be delivered up, killed, and rise.
basic.god: The Father openly declares and commands allegiance to His Son. God's values overturn the world's: the last is first, the servant is great, the child is welcomed, and sin is deadly serious.
basic.crossReferences: Exodus 24 and 34 describe glory on the mountain. Malachi 4 promises Elijah. Isaiah 66 supplies the undying worm and unquenchable fire.
basic.oneStory: On the way to the cross, heaven pulls back the curtain: the suffering Son is the glorious Son of God, and the Father commands us to heed Him. His followers, still grasping for greatness, must learn the upside-down way of the kingdom, service, humility, and ruthless holiness, the way of the One who came not to be served but to serve, and to give His life.

context.literary:
The scene is set between two sayings about the cross and glory. In Mark 8:34 to 9:1 Jesus has told the crowd to take up their cross and has promised that some standing there would see the kingdom come with power. Mark then dates the mountain scene with the odd note 'after six days,' so the vision reads as the first answer to that promise, and the voice of the Father stands over the whole central section, 8:27 to 10:45. That section is built on three predictions of the Passion, 8:31, 9:31 and 10:33, and each is followed by a failure of understanding and a lesson in discipleship. Here the failure is a quarrel about greatness, 9:33 to 34.

Mark gives the Father's voice twice, at the baptism and here. In 1:11 it speaks to Jesus, 'You are My beloved Son.' In 9:7 it speaks to the disciples, 'This is My beloved Son,' and adds a command. What was once private confirmation becomes public instruction.

The mountain and the valley are set in contrast. On the heights Jesus is radiant and the disciples are terrified and talk nonsense, 9:6. At the foot of the mountain the other disciples are unable to help a boy and are argued over by scribes, 9:14 to 18. The glory above does not float free of the pain below; Jesus comes straight down into it.

The closing section, verses 33 to 50, is held together less by plot than by catchwords. 'In My name' links verses 37, 38, 39 and 41. 'Stumble' links verses 42 to 47. 'Fire' joins hell to the salting of verse 49, and 'salt' carries on into verse 50, so that the discourse ends with an image of ordinary kitchen use and a plain call to peace.
context.historical:
Mark does not name the mountain. Caesarea Philippi lies at the foot of Mount Hermon, and the previous scene, 8:27, was set in that district, so a spur of Hermon is the more natural setting. Tabor is the traditional choice, but nothing in the text decides between the two; it says only that they were led up a high mountain by themselves. Peter's offer to build shelters, 9:5, would have sounded natural to someone who knew the tent of meeting, Exodus 33:7 to 11, was the place God spoke with Moses.

The scribes taught that Elijah would return before the end, from Malachi 4:5. The disciples knew this and raise it at once, 9:11, because the three had just seen Elijah and did not know how to fit him with a Messiah who must suffer and be raised.

In the valley Mark describes a boy with symptoms that were later given medical names, but Mark and the father speak of a spirit, 9:17 and 25, and Jesus addresses it directly. Jesus' disciples had been given authority over unclean spirits in 6:7 and had used it in 6:13, so their failure in 9:18 is a shock.

A child had no legal or social standing. A child was someone to be fed and protected, not honoured, and a child could give nothing back. That is why picking up a child in His arms, 9:36, is an acted parable. Gehenna was the Valley of Hinnom beside Jerusalem. Jeremiah 7:31 says Israelites burned their sons and daughters there, and by the first century the name was used for the place of final judgment. Salt was used on grain offerings, Leviticus 2:13, and as a preservative, and a stone or donkey-driven millstone was the heaviest ordinary object a village knew.
context.canonical:
The cloud, the glory and the six days recall Moses on Sinai, Exodus 24:15 to 18, and the shining of the face recalls Exodus 34:29 to 30. The Father's words combine Psalm 2:7 and Isaiah 42:1 with the promise of a prophet like Moses whom Israel must hear, Deuteronomy 18:15. Peter later returns to the scene as an eyewitness in 2 Peter 1:16 to 18, and Luke supplies the subject of the conversation, His departure, Luke 9:31, a word that the Old Testament reader hears as 'exodus.'

The Elijah thread runs back to Malachi 4:5 to 6, which closes the Old Testament with the promise of Elijah. Mark has already dressed John the Baptist like Elijah, Mark 1:6 and 2 Kings 1:8, and Jesus now says that Elijah has come and been mistreated, 9:13. The scene with the boy has Old Testament parallels in 1 Kings 17:17 to 24 and 2 Kings 4:32 to 37, where a prophet restores a dead child.

The warnings about hell take their language from the last verse of Isaiah, 66:24. Paul takes up the disciples' dispute in Philippians 2:3 to 8, where the pattern of Christ's self-emptying is held up against rivalry. John writes of glory in the flesh, John 1:14, and the later church read the mountain as a preview of what believers will be, Philippians 3:21.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
Mark wrote for believers who were likely facing pressure and the cost of following a crucified Messiah. He sets the glory of the mountain at the middle of his Gospel so that those who hear about the cross are not left thinking it is a defeat. The Father's voice settles who Jesus is, and its command, listen to Him, settles who has the final word, even over Moses and Elijah.

Mark is equally concerned with the disciples' failure. The Twelve are not villains; they are slow and afraid, and Mark leaves their quarrelling in plain view so that his readers will recognise themselves. The chain of sayings in verses 33 to 50 was meant to be remembered and repeated in the churches: receive the lowly, do not guard your own circle, take sin seriously, and keep the peace.

The boy's father is the quiet centre of the middle scene. Mark wanted readers to find in him a person who is honest enough to confess doubt and humble enough to ask for help, and to learn that Jesus responds to that.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
Some of this is unrepeatable. No disciple will see Jesus transfigured as the three did, and Mark presents the healing of the boy as an event, not a program. The Father's command, listen to Him, is for every believer. The reply about prayer in verse 29 is about the disciples' own dependence on God, not about a technique for exorcism.

The sayings about greatness, children, tolerance, stumbling and sin are written as instructions and are meant to be applied. The sayings about cutting off a hand or foot are a vivid way of putting a real command, and Mark's readers would have heard the exaggeration. The command is not to injure the body but to refuse sin whatever it costs. The statement that the one who is not against us is for us is not a licence to ignore doctrine, since Jesus ties it to someone acting in His name, verse 39.

debates.question: What does the father's cry, I believe, help my unbelief, teach about faith?

views.label: Faith and struggle can coexist
views.case: The father genuinely believes yet is honest about his weakness; Jesus honours his imperfect, growing faith, showing that faith need not be flawless to lay hold of Christ, only real and directed to Him.

views.label: Faith itself is a gift to be sought from Jesus
views.case: The man asks Jesus to help even his unbelief, acknowledging that the power and the faith alike come from Christ; genuine faith casts itself on Jesus not only for the miracle but for faith to believe.

debates.bearing: Both readings comfort weak believers: Jesus welcomes honest, struggling faith and is the one to whom we bring even our doubt, asking Him to strengthen it.

debates.question: Does Jesus command literal self-mutilation to avoid sin?

views.label: Vivid hyperbole for decisive action
views.case: Jesus uses shocking overstatement to convey that nothing, however precious, is worth clinging to if it drags us into sin; the point is ruthless, wholehearted repentance, not literal amputation, which would not cure a sinful heart.

views.label: A sober measure of eternal stakes
views.case: The extremity of the language matches the extremity of the danger, hell's unquenchable fire; better to lose anything now than to be lost forever, so the hyperbole presses the infinite worth of the soul.

debates.bearing: Both hold that the commands dramatize the seriousness of sin and the value of eternal life, calling for radical, inward dealing with sin rather than physical self-harm.

debates.question: Why Moses and Elijah, and why do they vanish?

views.label: The Law and the Prophets
views.case: Moses gave the Torah and Elijah is the great prophet of the later books, so the pair stand for the whole Old Testament witness. Their disappearance in verse 8 leaves Jesus alone, and the voice that tells the three to listen to Him places Him above both, much as Hebrews 1:1-2 sets the Son beside the prophets.

views.label: Two men who met God on the mountain and were not taken by an ordinary death
views.case: Both met God on a mountain, Moses at Sinai and Elijah at Horeb in 1 Kings 19. Elijah was taken up in a whirlwind, 2 Kings 2:11, and Deuteronomy 34:5-6 says the LORD buried Moses, so some hear them as figures who share the age to come. Luke adds that they spoke of His departure at Jerusalem, Luke 9:31.

views.label: Suffering prophets who were rejected
views.case: Moses was resisted by Israel and Elijah hunted by Jezebel. Their presence while Jesus is warning of rejection, Mark 8:31 and 9:12, ties His coming path to the way God's spokesmen had always been treated.

debates.bearing: These readings do not compete. Mark gives no interpretation himself, only the Father's command, so the safest conclusion is the one the text states: the old witnesses fall silent and the Son alone is to be heard.

study.originalLanguages:
In 9:7 the voice commands, 'listen to Him,' with the verb akouo in the present imperative. The tense gives the sense of ongoing, habitual hearing: keep on listening to Him. The wording is close to that of the Greek translation of Deuteronomy 18:15, where Israel is told to listen to the prophet like Moses, so the Father is saying that the prophet Moses promised has come. The word 'beloved,' agapetos, is also used in the Septuagint of Isaac, the son Abraham was asked to offer in Genesis 22:2, and in Mark's parable of the vineyard the owner's 'one beloved son,' Mark 12:6, is the one sent and killed. The title carries the shadow of sacrifice before the first hearer gets to the cross.

Peter proposes three 'shelters,' skenai, 9:5. The word is the one the Septuagint uses for the tent of meeting and the tabernacle, and when the cloud comes it 'overshadows' them, the verb episkiazo. The Septuagint uses the same verb in Exodus 40:35 of the cloud over the tabernacle, so the vocabulary says that God has pitched His own tent and does not need Peter's.

When the disciples ask about Elijah, Jesus says he 'restores all things,' 9:12. The verb apokathistano (apokathistemi) is the one the Septuagint of Malachi 4:6 uses for Elijah's work of turning hearts, so Jesus is quoting the expectation and then reinterpreting it: restoration is real but costs the prophet his life.

In the valley the father says, 'if You can,' 9:22, and Jesus throws the phrase back with an article, so that it reads something like 'that 'if You can'!' The answer, 'all things are possible,' uses the adjective dynata, which Jesus uses of God in 10:27 and prays to the Father in Gethsemane, 14:36. What is possible for God becomes possible for the one who believes by dependence on Him. The father's reply uses boetheo, 'help,' and apistia, 'unbelief,' the noun used of Nazareth in 6:6. In verse 22 he said 'help us'; in verse 24 he says 'help my unbelief,' as he moves from the group to himself.

Finally, after the spirit leaves, the boy is 'like a corpse,' nekros, and many say he is dead. Jesus 'raised him,' egeiro, and 'he stood up,' anistemi, 9:27. These are the verbs of resurrection that the disciples have just been puzzling over in 9:9 to 10 and 9:31. In 9:48 the worm that does not die and the fire not quenched, skolex and asbestos, follow the Septuagint of Isaiah 66:24 almost word for word.

typology.type: Sinai and the radiant face of Moses, Exodus 24 and 34
typology.fulfillment: Moses went up a mountain, a cloud covered it and the LORD spoke from within, Exodus 24:15 to 16, and when he came down his face shone so brightly that the people were afraid to come near, Exodus 34:29 to 30. At the transfiguration the glory is not reflected from Jesus but belongs to Him, and the cloud speaks about Him. Hebrews 12:18 to 24 draws the contrast between Sinai and the mountain Jesus brings people to. Moses' glory faded, 2 Corinthians 3:7 to 11; the glory of Christ is the pattern for believers, 2 Corinthians 3:18. The type falls short because Moses was a servant in the house, and Jesus is a Son over it, Hebrews 3:5 to 6.

typology.type: The tent of meeting and Peter's shelters, Exodus 40:34 to 35
typology.fulfillment: When the tabernacle was finished the cloud covered the tent and the glory filled it, Exodus 40:34 to 35. Peter's offer to build shelters shows an instinct that this is a sacred place, though Mark says he did not know what to say. John later says the Word 'made His dwelling among us' and that 'we have seen His glory,' John 1:14, using the language of tent-dwelling for the incarnation. The shelters are not needed because the presence is a person who walks down the mountain. The type falls short because a tabernacle could be entered by few and only briefly, while Christ's presence goes with His people to the valley and the cross.

typology.type: Elijah who must come, and John the Baptist, Malachi 4:5 to 6
typology.fulfillment: Jesus says that Elijah has come and that people did what they pleased to him, 9:13. Mark has prepared this by clothing John in the dress of Elijah, 1:6, and by recounting his death at Herod's hand, 6:17 to 29, much as Jezebel hunted Elijah, 1 Kings 19:2. Matthew states the identification, Matthew 17:13. The correspondence is that a prophet in Elijah's spirit calls Israel to turn back. The escalation is that his suffering announces the greater suffering of the Son of Man, 9:12. The type falls short because John, who told people that One stronger was coming, Mark 1:7, was a forerunner and not himself the one to be listened to.

typology.type: Prophets who restore a dead child, 1 Kings 17 and 2 Kings 4
typology.fulfillment: Elijah stretched himself over a dead boy three times and cried to the LORD, 1 Kings 17:21, and Elisha did something similar, 2 Kings 4:34 to 35. In Mark the boy is 'like a corpse,' and Jesus takes him by the hand and raises him with a word and no prayer-stretching, 9:27. The correspondence shows that Jesus acts in the line of the prophets, but the contrast shows He is more than a prophet: He does not ask God to give life, He gives it. Mark 5:41 shows the same gesture with Jairus's daughter. The type falls short in that this boy would die again, and the real answer lies in the One who 'will rise,' 9:31.

study.christ:
The chapter leads to Christ most directly by identity. The Father calls Jesus 'My beloved Son,' as at the baptism, Mark 1:11, and the title carries both royal weight, Psalm 2:7, and the shadow of the offered son, Genesis 22:2. Hebrews says the Son is 'the radiance of God's glory and the exact representation of His nature,' Hebrews 1:3, and on the mountain a little of that is allowed to show. Paul says the same glory is seen 'in the face of Jesus Christ,' 2 Corinthians 4:6. Jesus told His disciples only six days earlier that the Son of Man must suffer, Mark 8:31, and Peter could not bear it, 8:32 to 33. The vision is the Father's answer to that scandal: the one who goes to the cross is the glorious Son.

It leads to Christ by contrast with Moses and Elijah. They talk with Jesus, Luke says about His departure, Luke 9:31, and then they are gone, and no one is left with the three except Jesus, Mark 9:8. They pointed to a coming One, Deuteronomy 18:15 and Malachi 4:5. Now the voice says to hear Him, and Peter will later call himself a witness of that majesty, 2 Peter 1:16 to 18.

It leads to Christ by the pattern of descent. He comes down from glory to a boy in convulsions, takes him by the hand and raises him. Paul traces the same direction: the one 'existing in the form of God' emptied Himself and became obedient to death, Philippians 2:6 to 8. The same Jesus who can say 'all things are possible' also says that the Son of Man will be delivered into human hands, 9:23 and 31. The power is not set aside by the cross; it is the cross that is the power.

The words about greatness and children are not only instructions; they describe Him. He is the one who became last and servant of all, and who welcomes the lowly as welcoming Him and the One who sent Him, 9:35 to 37. The warnings of hell come from the One who in Gethsemane would ask whether the cup could pass and then drink it, Mark 14:36.

Caution is needed. The six days, the three disciples and the cloud are real details, but not every feature of the scene is a code. The links above rest on what the New Testament itself says about the scene, in Luke, Peter and John.
study.god:
The first thing the chapter shows is that God speaks. In the cloud the Father gives not an explanation but a command, and it is a command about attention. The God of Sinai who was heard in thunder, Hebrews 12:18 to 19, now directs His people to a Man. That fits what the chapter shows about the nature of God: He does not hide behind distance. He reveals Himself in His Son, and the disciples' task is to hear.

The Father shows both delight and authority. 'Beloved' is the language of love, and 'listen' is the language of rule; in this scene they are joined. A Father who loves His Son does not keep the Son's words to Himself.

The chapter also shows God's patience and knowledge. Jesus laments an unbelieving generation, 9:19, and yet He says, bring him to Me. He knows how long the boy has suffered and asks anyway, 9:21, as God asked questions in Eden. The Father knows the disciples were arguing even though they were silent, 9:33 to 34. Nothing in the quarrel is hidden from Him, and still He teaches them rather than dismissing them.

God is also holy and just. The warnings of verses 42 to 48 are among the sternest in the Gospels, and they come in a chapter that exalts a child. The same God who welcomes the small is angry with those who cause them to fall. Isaiah's picture of the worm and the fire, Isaiah 66:24, shows that God does not treat the final judgment lightly, and Jesus presses the point that any cost now is lighter than that.

He is the God who sends. Welcoming a child in Jesus' name is to welcome 'the One who sent Me,' 9:37, so the Father is behind the whole mission and is touched by how His Son is received.

For worship, the chapter suggests that reverent silence is a right response, since Peter spoke when he should not and the Father answered by speaking Himself. It also suggests that prayer is where those who serve a mighty God learn they have no power of their own, 9:29.

crossReferences.note: Moses goes up Sinai in a cloud, the glory settles on the mountain for six days and the LORD speaks on the seventh. Mark's dating, 'after six days,' and the cloud with a voice make the first hearers recall that event, but this time the speaking is about another Man.

Moses' face was radiant after speaking with the LORD, and the people feared to come near. Jesus' whole appearance changes and His clothes shine, and the three disciples are terrified, 9:6. Moses carried a reflected glory; the glory on the mountain is Jesus' own.

Moses promises a prophet like himself and tells Israel to listen to him. The Father's command in Mark 9:7, 'Listen to Him!', takes the same verb and places Jesus as the prophet who was promised, so that He, not Moses, is the voice to follow.

The Old Testament ends with the promise of Elijah before the Day of the LORD. Jesus' answer in 9:12 to 13 treats the promise as fulfilled in John the Baptist, who was received with violence, and joins it to the Son of Man's own coming suffering.

Peter writes as a surviving eyewitness of the majesty he saw on the holy mountain and heard in the voice from heaven. The apostle who in Mark spoke without knowing what to say now uses the scene as a plain proof that the Christian message is not a story made up by clever people.

Luke records what Mark leaves out: Moses and Elijah spoke of His departure, which He was about to accomplish at Jerusalem. The word is exodus in Greek, so the mountain conversation is about a new deliverance carried out through death, the very thing the disciples find hard to hear.

The Word made His dwelling among us, using the image of the tent, and the apostles saw His glory. The transfiguration is one of the moments when that glory broke through the ordinary appearance of Jesus, and it prepares readers to see glory in the incarnation itself.

The last verse of Isaiah speaks of the worm that does not die and the fire that is not quenched around those who rebelled. Jesus quotes it in Mark 9:48 to give the final stakes of sin, so His warning is not His own invention but drawn from the prophet's closing image.

Elijah restores the widow's son after stretching over the child and calling on the LORD. Jesus' raising of the boy in Mark 9:27 sits beside this story, and the difference lies in how He acts: with His own word, taking the hand and raising him up.

Paul sets Christ's emptying of Himself against selfish ambition. The disciples' argument over rank in Mark 9:34 is the problem Paul addresses, and the answer is the same: have the mind of the one who took the form of a servant and became obedient to death.

God spoke by the prophets in many ways, and has now spoken by His Son, who is the radiance of His glory. The passage reads like a commentary on the mountain: the prophets fall away, and the Son is the final word, so that the Father's command in Mark 9:7 has its reason.

study.oneStory:
The Bible begins with a world that carried the glory of God and humans made to bear His image. After the fall that glory is veiled, and the story from then on is a search for how God will dwell with a people again. The tabernacle and temple are partial answers, and Moses sees only a glimpse of the glory on Sinai, Exodus 33:18 to 23. Elijah meets the LORD on the same mountain after fleeing in despair, 1 Kings 19:8 to 12, and the prophets keep pointing to a day when God will come Himself.

In Mark 9 a small part of that day arrives. For a few moments the three see what the Son of Man really is, and they hear the Father give the promised prophet to His people. The chapter then turns at once to the valley, because the glory is on its way to a cross. The way down is the way to Jerusalem, where the same disciples who now want rank will watch Him die.

The chapter also fits the larger shape of the Bible by showing what the new age is like. The first Adam grasped at greatness and fell. The Son, in the form of God, does not grasp but serves, and He tells His people to follow by receiving the small, guarding the weak, and refusing what ruins them. The salt of the closing verses recalls covenant offerings, and the call to peace is the life of a community that belongs to the kingdom.

And it points ahead. Paul says Christ 'will transform our lowly bodies to be like His glorious body,' Philippians 3:21, so the radiance seen on the mountain is not a private privilege but the destiny of His people. In the new creation the city has no need of sun or moon, 'because the glory of God illuminates the city, and the Lamb is its lamp,' Revelation 21:23. The shelters Peter wanted to build give way to a city where God dwells with His people, and the prophets and law are fulfilled in the Son, who is heard and seen without fear.

quiz.q: What did the transfiguration reveal, and what did the Father command?

options.text: Jesus' hidden divine glory as the beloved Son, and the Father's command to listen to Him.
options.note: Mark 9:2-7; the glory confirms His identity and the voice commands obedience to Him.

options.text: That Jesus was a great prophet alongside Moses and Elijah.
options.note: Moses and Elijah fade and Jesus alone remains; He is far more than a prophet beside them.

options.text: Jesus shining in glory, confirming the message of the cross He had just taught.
options.note: True and important, but it should name the Father's command, listen to Him, and Jesus as beloved Son.

options.text: That the disciples should build three shelters to stay on the mountain.
options.note: Peter's suggestion was mistaken; the point was the glory of the Son and the Father's command.

quiz.q: What does the father's cry, I do believe, help my unbelief, show?

options.text: That real but struggling faith can lay hold of Jesus, who welcomes honest, imperfect trust.
options.note: Mark 9:24; Jesus honours the man's genuine yet weak faith and heals his son.

options.text: That the man had no faith at all.
options.note: He says I do believe; his faith was real though mixed with weakness.

options.text: That faith and doubt can exist together in a sincere heart seeking Jesus.
options.note: True, but the fuller point is that Jesus welcomes and strengthens such honest, imperfect faith.

options.text: That faith must be perfect before Jesus will act.
options.note: The opposite; Jesus acts for a man whose faith is admittedly imperfect.

quiz.q: How does Jesus define true greatness?

options.text: To be first, one must be the last of all and the servant of all.
options.note: Mark 9:35; greatness in the kingdom is lowly service.

options.text: By welcoming children and the lowly in Jesus' name.
options.note: A true expression of it, but the core statement is that the first must be servant of all.

options.text: By achieving the most impressive works for God.
options.note: Jesus measures greatness by humble service, not by impressive achievement.

options.text: By ruling over others as the world's leaders do.
options.note: Jesus overturns that model; the great must serve, not lord it over others.

quiz.q: What is the point of Jesus' shocking words about cutting off a hand or plucking out an eye?

options.text: Vivid hyperbole urging radical, decisive dealing with sin, since eternal life is worth losing anything to gain.
options.note: The extreme images press the seriousness of sin and the worth of entering life, not literal mutilation.

options.text: A literal command to remove body parts that sin.
options.note: It is deliberate overstatement; mutilation could not cure a sinful heart.

options.text: A call to take sin with utmost seriousness because the stakes are eternal.
options.note: Correct in substance, but it should recognize the language as hyperbole urging decisive action.

options.text: A suggestion that sin is not really that dangerous.
options.note: The opposite; the extremity of the language shows how gravely dangerous sin is.

quiz.q: What does Jesus mean by calling His disciples to have salt among themselves?

options.text: To have a purifying, preserving character and to be at peace with one another rather than rivals for greatness.
options.note: Mark 9:50 ties salt to peace, answering their argument about who was greatest.

options.text: To add flavour to their conversations.
options.note: Salt here signifies purifying character and peace, not merely lively talk.

options.text: To live distinct, godly lives that influence the world around them.
options.note: A true dimension of being salt, but here Jesus specifically links it to peace among themselves.

options.text: To perform religious rituals with salt.
options.note: Jesus speaks of character and peace, not ritual.

questions: The Father said of Jesus, listen to Him. In what area of your life is Jesus asking to be heard and obeyed rather than merely admired?
The father prayed, I believe, help my unbelief. How might that honest prayer give you courage to bring your own struggling faith to Jesus?
The disciples argued about greatness while Jesus spoke of dying. Where do you catch yourself competing for status instead of seeking to serve?
Jesus said welcoming a lowly child is welcoming Him. Who are the overlooked or unimportant people God is calling you to receive in His name?
Jesus urged radical action against whatever leads to sin. What specific thing might you need to cut off decisively for the sake of your walk with God?

translationNotes.note: This kind cannot come out except by prayer; some manuscripts add and fasting. Either way Jesus locates the disciples' failure in prayerless self-reliance rather than a wrong technique.

The BSB does not print verses 44 and 46, since the words repeated there, their worm never dies and the fire is never quenched, are not in the earliest manuscripts and are already given in verse 48; the numbering therefore skips 44 and 46.
Their worm never dies, and the fire is never quenched quotes Isaiah 66:24, a picture of final judgment that Jesus applies to gehenna, hell.
